variables-assignment.name: Assign and reassign names
variables-assignment.useWhen: a value must be stored, updated or kept for later
variables-assignment.pitfall: Assigning one name never changes another name
useCases: Keep a running score that changes each round
Remember the old price before applying a discount
Swap the values of two variables
Count how many times a button was clicked
Store a player name typed by the user
Save the starting level before the game changes it

numbers-int-float.name: Whole and decimal numbers
numbers-int-float.useWhen: you divide, round or compare decimal numbers
numbers-int-float.template:
<a> / <b>            // keeps the fraction
Math.trunc(<x>)       // drops it
numbers-int-float.pitfall: Decimal sums like 0.1 + 0.2 are not exact
useCases: Split a bill evenly between friends
Work out an average score
Round a price to whole euros
Check whether two measured lengths are equal
Turn 7.9 hours into whole hours worked
Compute a percentage of a total

str-vs-number.name: Text versus number values
str-vs-number.useWhen: values come from text: forms, files, query strings
str-vs-number.rule: + joins when either side is text; other math converts.
str-vs-number.howItRuns: '3' + 4 makes '34'; '3' - 1 makes 2; Number('3') turns text into a real number.
str-vs-number.pitfall: Form inputs are text even when they hold digits
useCases: Add two quantities typed into a form
Sort version numbers stored as text
Build an order code from two parts
Read an age from a query string and add one
Compare a typed answer with a numeric solution
Total the numbers read from a CSV line

string-indexing.name: Index into a string
string-indexing.useWhen: you need one character at a known position
string-indexing.pitfall: The last index is length - 1; [-1] finds nothing
useCases: Get the first letter of a name for an avatar
Check whether a sentence ends with a period
Read the check digit at the end of a code
Build initials from a first and last name
Find the middle character of a word
Test whether a file name starts with a dot

string-methods.name: Call string methods
string-methods.useWhen: text must be cleaned, changed or searched
string-methods.pitfall: Methods return a new string; keep the result
useCases: Clean the spaces around a typed email address
Compare two words ignoring upper and lower case
Replace a placeholder word in a message
Turn a title into a shouting headline
Remove the newline at the end of a line
Censor every copy of a banned word

string-formatting.name: Format values into text
string-formatting.useWhen: values must be shown inside text, aligned or rounded
useCases: Show a price with exactly two decimals
Build a greeting that includes the user name
Line up names in a column of a receipt
Print a progress message like 3 of 10
Pad order numbers with leading zeros
Show a percentage rounded to one decimal

comparison-equality.name: Compare values
comparison-equality.useWhen: you order or match strings and numbers
comparison-equality.pitfall: Strings compare letter by letter, capitals before lowercase
useCases: Check whether a word comes before another alphabetically
Test whether a temperature lies inside a range
Sort a list of names
Check a typed password against the stored one
Find the earlier of two dates written as text
Compare a score with the high score

conditionals.name: Branch with if and else
conditionals.pitfall: Only the first true branch of a chain runs
useCases: Give a grade letter for a score
Pick a shipping price by order weight
Show a weather message for a temperature
Apply a discount only to members
Check whether a day is a weekend day
Choose a greeting by the hour of the day

booleans-truthiness.name: Truthy and falsy values
booleans-truthiness.useWhen: a condition tests a value that is not true or false
booleans-truthiness.rule: Falsy: false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, NaN. All else truthy.
booleans-truthiness.howItRuns: if and || convert the value to true or false; || and && then hand back one of the values.
useCases: Show a fallback title when the title is empty
Skip an empty shopping cart
Use a default page size when none is given
Check whether a search returned any results
Keep a count of zero instead of replacing it
Decide whether a form field was filled in

for-range-bounds.name: Count with a range loop
for-range-bounds.useWhen: something must repeat a known number of times
for-range-bounds.pitfall: i < end stops before end; <= includes it
useCases: Print the numbers 1 to 10
Visit every index of an array
Repeat a drawing step five times
Count down from 10 to 1
Take every second item of a list
Build a row of n stars

loop-accumulator.name: Accumulate in a loop
loop-accumulator.useWhen: you need one result built from every item
loop-accumulator.template:
let total = <start>;
for (const <x> of <xs>) total = total <op> <x>;
loop-accumulator.pitfall: Set the starting value once, before the loop
useCases: Add up the prices in a shopping cart
Count the words longer than five letters
Find the highest temperature of the week
Join names into one comma-separated string
Multiply all the numbers in a list together
Total the minutes of a playlist

list-indexing.name: Index into a list
list-indexing.useWhen: you need the item at a known position
list-indexing.pitfall: The last index is length - 1; [-1] finds nothing
useCases: Get the first player in a turn order
Read the newest entry at the end of a log
Swap the first and last items of a list
Check the runner-up in a ranked list
Read a value from a fixed column position
Get the middle reading of a sorted list

list-slicing.name: Slice a sequence
list-slicing.useWhen: you need a run of items from an array or string
list-slicing.pitfall: The item at the end index is never included
useCases: Take the first three scores from a list
Drop the header row from a list of lines
Get the last two characters of a file name
Keep a list without its first and last items
Split a list into a first half and a second half
Show one page of ten results

list-mutation-methods.name: Change a list in place
list-mutation-methods.useWhen: an array must grow or shrink in place
list-mutation-methods.pitfall: push returns the new length, not the array
useCases: Add a new message to a chat history
Undo the last action from a history list
Serve the first customer in a queue
Collect the even numbers into a new array
Add several rows to a table at once
Remove the oldest reading when the list is full

alias-copy.name: Aliases share one object
alias-copy.useWhen: two names might point at the same array or object
alias-copy.rule: Assignment never copies: both names share one array.
alias-copy.howItRuns: b = a makes b another name for the same array; changes through either name show in both.
alias-copy.pitfall: Copy with [...a] before changing an array you must keep
useCases: Keep the original list while sorting a copy
Pass an array to a function without it being changed
Store snapshots of a list for an undo history
Build a grid whose rows change independently
Reset a game board to its starting layout
Compare a list before and after editing it

function-def-call.name: Define and call a function
function-def-call.useWhen: the same steps are needed in several places
function-def-call.pitfall: Without () the function is named, not called
useCases: Compute the area of several rectangles
Format every price on a page the same way
Check whether a password is long enough
Convert temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit
Greet each user by name
Reuse a discount rule at checkout

function-return-vs-print.name: Return a value, not print
function-return-vs-print.useWhen: a function computes a value other code needs
function-return-vs-print.pitfall: console.log shows a value; only return hands it back
useCases: Compute a total that a later line adds tax to
Find the largest score and store it
Check a condition and use the answer in an if
Build a label string to show in two places
Stop searching as soon as a match is found
Convert units and feed the result to another function

closure-late-binding.name: Closures read variables late
closure-late-binding.useWhen: functions made in a loop run after the loop
closure-late-binding.rule: Closures read a variable when they run, not when made.
closure-late-binding.howItRuns: var gives the whole loop one shared i; let gives each pass its own i for its closures.
closure-late-binding.pitfall: Use let, not var, for loop counters used in callbacks
useCases: Attach a click handler to each button in a loop
Schedule several timers that each print their number
Build a list of functions that each remember an index
Create one callback per row of a table
Delay messages in a loop with setTimeout
Collect getter functions for each item

reading-tracebacks.name: Read a traceback
reading-tracebacks.useWhen: a program stops with an error and a stack trace
reading-tracebacks.template:
TypeError: <message>
    at <fn> (pad:<line>:<col>)   // failed here
    at pad:<line>:<col>          // called from here
reading-tracebacks.pitfall: The first at line is where it failed
useCases: Find which line crashed with a TypeError
Tell a typo in a name from a missing property
See which call passed a bad argument
Fix a function that reads a property of undefined
Understand a RangeError from a negative count
Trace an error back from a helper to its caller

null-undefined.name: Null versus undefined
null-undefined.useWhen: a value may be missing, unset or cleared
null-undefined.rule: Missing is undefined; null is an empty value set on purpose.
null-undefined.howItRuns: Unset variables and missing properties read as undefined; null appears only where code stores it.
null-undefined.pitfall: typeof null is 'object', so test null with === null
useCases: Read an optional setting that may be missing
Show a fallback name when a nickname is empty
Tell a cleared field from one never filled
Sum values when some entries are missing
Check whether a lookup found anything
Give a function parameter a default value

loose-vs-strict-equality.name: Strict equality with ===
loose-vs-strict-equality.useWhen: you compare values that may have different types
loose-vs-strict-equality.rule: === compares type and value; == converts types first.
loose-vs-strict-equality.howItRuns: '5' == 5 converts the text and says true; '5' === 5 sees two types and says false.
loose-vs-strict-equality.pitfall: NaN is never equal to anything, not even NaN
useCases: Check a typed answer against a numeric solution
Test whether a value is null or undefined
Detect a failed number conversion
Compare an id from a URL with a stored id
Check whether an optional setting was given
Decide whether a count of zero means missing

let-const-var-scope.name: Block scope: let and const
let-const-var-scope.useWhen: you declare a name and decide where it may be used
let-const-var-scope.template:
const <name> = <value>;   // never reassigned
let <name> = <value>;     // reassigned, block-scoped
let-const-var-scope.pitfall: const fixes the name, not the contents of the object
useCases: Keep a loop counter from leaking out of the loop
Declare a list you will push items into
Track a running total that changes
Use a temporary value inside one if block
Avoid accidentally reusing a name from outer code
Mark a setting that must never be reassigned

array-map-filter-reduce.name: Map, filter and reduce
array-map-filter-reduce.useWhen: you transform, select or combine every item of an array
array-map-filter-reduce.pitfall: An arrow with braces needs an explicit return
useCases: Double every price in a list
Keep only the passing scores
Add up the lengths of all words
Turn a list of users into a list of names
Drop empty lines from a file
Find the longest word with one pass

object-property-access.name: Access object properties
object-property-access.useWhen: you read or write a named property of an object
object-property-access.template:
<obj>.<name>        // fixed name
<obj>[<variable>]   // name held in a variable
object-property-access.pitfall: obj.key never reads the variable key
useCases: Read a setting whose name the user picked
Count votes per candidate in an object
Read a nested city from a user address
Look up a price by product code
Update one field of a record
Safely read a property that may be missing

this-method-call.name: this in method calls
this-method-call.useWhen: a method reads or changes its own object
this-method-call.pitfall: A method stored in a variable loses its this
useCases: Pass an object method as a click handler
Let a counter object increase its own count
Chain deposit calls on a bank account object
Use a method inside an array callback
Store a method in a variable to call later
Read an object setting from inside its method

type-annotations.name: Type annotations are erased
type-annotations.useWhen: you describe what types values should have
type-annotations.pitfall: Annotations are erased; they never check or convert values
useCases: Describe the shape of a parsed JSON object
Mark which arguments a function expects
Catch a wrong argument type before running
Convert a form value that tsc thinks is a number
Guard unknown input with a typeof check
Document the return type of a helper

transforms.belief: console.log shows a value assigned on a later line
transforms.refutation: Lines run top to bottom: the first console.log prints before the next line assigns the new value.
transforms.rule: Each line runs in order; later lines cannot change earlier output.

transforms.belief: After b = a, reassigning a also changes b
transforms.refutation: let {{@b}} = {{@a}} copies the number; reassigning {{@a}} later points only {{@a}} at a new value.
transforms.rule: Reassigning one name never changes another name.

transforms.belief: a = b then b = a swaps the two values
transforms.refutation: After {{@a}} = {{@b}} runs, {{@a}} already holds the value of {{@b}}, so the next line copies that same value back.
transforms.rule: Swapping needs a temporary name to keep the old value.

transforms.belief: After b = a, reassigning a also changes b
transforms.refutation: {{@b}} was computed once, when it was declared; changing {{@a}} afterwards does not recompute it.
transforms.rule: A computed value stays fixed until you assign it again.

templates.harness:
check(JSON.stringify({{@fn}}([{{x}}, {{y}}])) === '[{{y}},{{x}}]', 'swaps two numbers');
check(JSON.stringify({{@fn}}([{{y}}, {{z}}])) === '[{{z}},{{y}}]', 'swaps another pair');

transforms.belief: Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number
transforms.refutation: JavaScript has one number type, and / keeps the fraction. Only Math.floor or Math.trunc would drop it.
transforms.rule: / always keeps the fraction; Math.floor drops it.

transforms.belief: 0.1 + 0.2 equals exactly 0.3
transforms.refutation: Decimals like 0.{{x}} are stored as tiny binary approximations, so their sum lands a hair away from 0.{{z}}.
transforms.rule: Compare decimals after rounding, never with ===.

transforms.belief: Converting 2.7 to a whole number rounds it to 3
transforms.refutation: Math.trunc chops off the decimals and never rounds, however close the value is to the next number.
transforms.rule: Math.trunc drops decimals; Math.round rounds.

transforms.belief: Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number
transforms.refutation: {{w}} is odd, and / keeps the half: JavaScript has one number type, so whole numbers can divide into fractions.
transforms.rule: / always keeps the fraction; Math.floor drops it.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}, {{b}}]) === {{h}}.5, 'averages to a half');
check({{@fn}}([{{c}}, {{d}}]) === {{g}}.5, 'averages another pair');

transforms.belief: '2' + '3' adds them to make 5
transforms.refutation: Both values are text in quotes, so + joins them side by side instead of adding them.
transforms.rule: + on two strings joins them; convert with Number first.

transforms.belief: Adding a number to digit text does arithmetic
transforms.refutation: When either side of + is text, JavaScript turns the number into text and joins them; only - forces arithmetic.
transforms.rule: + with any string joins text; - always does math.

transforms.belief: '10' < '9' compares them as numbers
transforms.refutation: Text compares character by character from the left, so the first characters decide before length matters.
transforms.rule: Strings compare letter by letter; convert to numbers first.

templates.rule: + joins strings; use Number() first to add them.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}(['{{a}}', '{{b}}']) === {{s1}}, 'adds two quantities');
check({{@fn}}(['{{c}}', '{{d}}', '{{e}}']) === {{s2}}, 'adds three quantities');

transforms.belief: Comparing two strings compares their lengths
transforms.refutation: Strings compare like a dictionary: the first differing letter decides, and length only matters when one word is a prefix.
transforms.rule: Strings compare letter by letter, like dictionary order.

transforms.belief: Capital letters compare as bigger than lowercase ones
transforms.refutation: Default sort compares character codes, and every capital letter has a smaller code than every lowercase letter.
transforms.rule: Capitals sort before lowercase; compare lowercase copies for alphabetical order.

transforms.belief: == and === always give the same answer
transforms.refutation: == converts the text to a number before comparing; only === refuses to convert, so the two lines differ.
transforms.rule: == converts types first; === compares type and value.

transforms.belief: '1' === 1 is true
transforms.refutation: === never converts: text and a number are different types, so they are never strictly equal.
transforms.rule: === needs the same type and the same value.

transforms.belief: NaN === NaN is true
transforms.refutation: Converting a word with Number gives NaN, the one value that is never equal to anything, itself included.
transforms.rule: NaN never equals itself; test it with Number.isNaN.

transforms.belief: null == 0 is true
transforms.refutation: == treats null as equal only to null and undefined; it never converts null to a number, unlike >=.
transforms.rule: null == only matches null and undefined.

transforms.belief: == and === always give the same answer
transforms.refutation: == counts null and undefined as equal, while === sees two different values.
transforms.rule: == converts types first; === compares type and value.

templates.code:
const {{@a}}: any = '{{x}}';
console.log({{@a}} == {{x}});
templates.rule: === never converts types; == converts before comparing.

transforms.belief: A missing property is null
transforms.refutation: {{@obj}} has no {{@other}} property; JavaScript only gives null where some code stored null on purpose.
transforms.rule: Missing properties are undefined; null is only set on purpose.

transforms.belief: undefined + 1 gives 1
transforms.refutation: undefined is not zero: arithmetic with it cannot produce a real number. Give it a default with ?? first.
transforms.rule: Default missing values with ?? before doing math.

transforms.belief: typeof null gives 'null'
transforms.refutation: typeof null is a historical quirk and does not name null; test for null with === null instead.
transforms.rule: Check for null with === null, not with typeof.

transforms.belief: null === undefined is true
transforms.refutation: null and undefined are two different values; only the loose == treats them as equal.
transforms.rule: === keeps null and undefined apart; == lumps them together.

transforms.belief: undefined + 1 gives 1
transforms.refutation: {{@total}} starts as undefined, not zero, so the very first += already spoils the sum.
transforms.rule: Start a running total at 0, never undefined.

templates.code:
const {{@obj}}: Record<string, null> = { {{@key}}: null };
console.log({{@obj}}.{{@key}}, {{n}});
templates.rule: A missing property is undefined; null is stored on purpose.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}({}) === {{dflt}}, 'uses the default when missing');
check({{@fn}}({ {{@prop}}: {{v}} }) === {{v}}, 'keeps a given value');

transforms.belief: Every branch whose condition is true runs
transforms.refutation: else if is only checked when every condition above it was false; the first true branch ends the chain.
transforms.rule: In an if/else chain only the first true branch runs.

transforms.belief: Separate ifs act like elif: only one runs
transforms.refutation: Two separate if statements are checked one after the other; without else, the second runs whether or not the first did.
transforms.rule: Separate ifs are all checked; only else makes them exclusive.

transforms.belief: x == 'a' or 'b' compares x with both
transforms.refutation: || joins two separate conditions; '{{y}}' on its own is a non-empty string, which always counts as true.
transforms.rule: Repeat the variable: x === 'a' || x === 'b'.

transforms.belief: An empty array counts as false in an if
transforms.refutation: Every array is an object, and objects are always truthy, even with nothing inside; only its length can be zero.
transforms.rule: Every array is truthy; test emptiness with .length.

transforms.belief: The string '0' counts as false
transforms.refutation: Only the empty string is falsy; '0' holds one character, so it counts as true until Number converts it.
transforms.rule: Non-empty strings are truthy, even '0' and 'false'.

transforms.belief: and / or always give a boolean, never one of the values
transforms.refutation: || hands back one of its two values, the first truthy one, rather than a plain true or false.
transforms.rule: a || b gives back a or b itself.

transforms.belief: and / or always give a boolean, never one of the values
transforms.refutation: && hands back one of its values: the first falsy one, or the last value when both are truthy.
transforms.rule: a && b gives back a or b itself.

templates.code:
const {{@xs}}: number[] = [];
console.log({{@xs}}.length ? '{{@full}}' : '{{@empty}}', {{n}});
templates.rule: Every array is truthy; test emptiness with .length.

transforms.belief: const makes an object's contents unchangeable
transforms.refutation: const only stops {{@list}} from being pointed at another array; the array itself can still change.
transforms.rule: const fixes the name, not the contents.

transforms.belief: A let inside a block is visible after it
transforms.refutation: The inner let creates a second {{@x}} that lives only inside the braces; the outer {{@x}} is untouched.
transforms.rule: A let inside braces disappears when the block ends.

transforms.belief: A var inside a block disappears after the block
transforms.refutation: A var loop counter is not limited to the loop; i survives after it, holding the value that ended the loop.
transforms.rule: var ignores blocks; let and const stay inside them.

transforms.belief: Using a let before its line gives undefined
transforms.refutation: A let exists only from its own line onward; the first call reads {{@second}} too early, which is an error, not a missing value.
transforms.rule: Declare let and const before any code that uses them runs.

subgoals.label: i exists only in the loop

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}]) === {{b}}, 'finds the largest');
check({{@fn}}([{{c}}, {{a}}, {{e}}]) === {{e}}, 'finds another largest');

transforms.belief: The first item is at position 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: Indexes count from zero, so [{{i}}] and [{{j}}] name characters one place further along than counting from one suggests.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first character.

transforms.belief: The last item is at index len, not len - 1
transforms.refutation: A string of length n has indexes zero to n - 1, so the last character sits one before the length.
transforms.rule: The last character is at length - 1.

transforms.belief: Index -1 gives the last item
transforms.refutation: Square brackets never count from the end: [-1] looks for a position named -1, which no string has. Use .at(-1).
transforms.rule: [-1] finds nothing; .at(-1) gives the last character.

transforms.belief: The first item is at position 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: Positions start at zero, so [1] and [2] are the second and third characters of {{@code}}.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first character.

transforms.belief: You can change one character with s[0] = 'x'
transforms.refutation: Strings cannot be changed in place; assigning to [0] is silently ignored. Build a new string instead.
transforms.rule: Strings never change; build a new one with slice.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([{{@ex}}]) === '{{@exp}}', 'takes the last letter of each word');
check({{@fn}}(['{{w}}']) === '{{w}}'.slice(-1), 'works for one word');

transforms.belief: A method like upper changes the string itself
transforms.refutation: Strings never change in place: toUpperCase returns a new string, and the bare call throws that result away.
transforms.rule: String methods return new strings; assign the result to keep it.

transforms.belief: replace with a string changes every match
transforms.refutation: With a string pattern, replace changes only the first match; replaceAll is needed for every match.
transforms.rule: replace changes the first match; replaceAll changes them all.

transforms.belief: A method like upper changes the string itself
transforms.refutation: replace builds a new string, stored in {{@fixed}}; {{@text}} itself is never changed.
transforms.rule: String methods return new strings; the original stays the same.

transforms.belief: strip/trim also removes spaces inside the text
transforms.refutation: trim removes spaces only from the two ends; the space between the words stays.
transforms.rule: trim cleans both ends, never the middle.

transforms.belief: A method like upper changes the string itself
transforms.refutation: trim returns a new string; {{@raw}} keeps all of its spaces, so the two strings differ.
transforms.rule: String methods return new strings; the original stays the same.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}('  {{@up}} ') === '{{@low}}', 'trims and lowercases');
check({{@fn}}(' {{w}}  ') === '{{w}}', 'already lowercase');

transforms.belief: ${name} fills in inside normal quotes too
transforms.refutation: Only backtick strings fill in ${...}; inside single quotes those characters are printed exactly as typed.
transforms.rule: ${} works only inside backticks.

transforms.belief: Formatting to 2 decimals just cuts off the extra digits
transforms.refutation: toFixed rounds to the nearest hundredth, so a third decimal of five or more pushes the second decimal up.
transforms.rule: toFixed rounds, and it returns a string.

transforms.belief: Padding to a width also cuts longer text
transforms.refutation: padStart only adds characters until the width is reached; text already longer than {{width}} is left whole.
transforms.rule: Padding only adds characters, never removes them.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}('tea', {{a}}) === 'tea... {{a}}.00', 'pads a short name');
check({{@fn}}('coffee', {{b}}.5) === 'coffee {{b}}.50', 'keeps a long name whole');

transforms.belief: The loop also runs for the end value
transforms.refutation: The loop keeps going only while i < {{n}} holds, so it stops before i reaches {{n}}.
transforms.rule: i < end stops before end; use <= to include it.

transforms.belief: Counting starts at 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: i starts at whatever value the loop header gives it, which is 0 here, and the test i < {{n}} stops it early.
transforms.rule: The loop starts at the value given, often 0.

transforms.belief: The loop also runs for the end value
transforms.refutation: The test is i < length, so the last pass uses the index just below the length; the length itself is never an index.
transforms.rule: i < length visits every index exactly once.

transforms.belief: A loop with a step always lands on the end value
transforms.refutation: Steps of {{step}} jump from 0 by fixed amounts; {{end}} is not a multiple of {{step}}, so no step lands on it.
transforms.rule: A stepped loop stops at the last step below the end.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}(1, {{n}}) === {{s1}}, 'adds 1 up to n, end included');
check({{@fn}}({{a}}, {{b}}) === {{s2}}, 'adds a middle range, end included');

transforms.belief: total = x adds x to the total
transforms.refutation: = replaces the total with the current item on each pass; += adds the item to what is already there.
transforms.rule: Use += to add each item to the total.

transforms.belief: Setting the total inside the loop still keeps a running sum
transforms.refutation: The reset line runs on every pass, so the total is wiped back to zero just before each item is added.
transforms.rule: Set the starting value once, before the loop.

transforms.belief: Starting the best value at 0 works for any numbers
transforms.refutation: Every value here is below zero, so none of them ever beats the starting 0; start from the first item instead.
transforms.rule: Start a maximum at the first item, not 0.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}], {{lim}}) === {{e1}}, 'adds only the values above the limit');
check({{@fn}}([{{b}}, {{c}}, {{b}}], 0) === {{e2}}, 'adds every value when all are above the limit');

transforms.belief: The first item is at position 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: Indexes count from zero, so [{{i}}] and [{{j}}] name items one place further along than counting from one suggests.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: The last item is at index len, not len - 1
transforms.refutation: An array of length n has indexes zero to n - 1, so the last item sits one before the length.
transforms.rule: The last item is at length - 1.

transforms.belief: Index -1 gives the last item
transforms.refutation: Square brackets never count from the end: [-1] looks for an item named -1, which arrays lack. Use .at(-1).
transforms.rule: [-1] finds nothing; .at(-1) gives the last item.

transforms.belief: The first item is at position 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: Positions start at zero, so [1] is the second item of {{@xs}}, not the first.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: The last item is at index len, not len - 1
transforms.refutation: The last item is at length - 1; reading at length itself would be past the end.
transforms.rule: The last item is at length - 1.

transforms.belief: The slice includes the item at the stop index
transforms.refutation: The end index is left out: slice({{i}}, {{j}}) takes the items at indexes {{i}} up to, but not including, {{j}}.
transforms.rule: slice includes the start index and excludes the end.

transforms.belief: The first item is at position 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: Indexes count from zero: the first item is index zero, so index {{i}} is one item further along.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.replace: throw new RangeError('slice end {{big}} is past the end');
transforms.belief: Slicing past the end raises an error
transforms.refutation: slice never complains about a range past the end; it simply stops at the last item that exists.
transforms.rule: slice clamps out-of-range ends instead of raising errors.

transforms.belief: The first item is at position 1, not 0
transforms.refutation: Indexes count from zero, so slice({{i}}, ...) starts {{i}} items after the first one.
transforms.rule: Index 0 is the first item.

transforms.belief: Changing a slice also changes the original list
transforms.refutation: slice copies the chosen items into a brand-new array, so changing {{@part}} leaves {{@xs}} alone.
transforms.rule: slice returns a new array; the original is untouched.

transforms.belief: Adding an item gives back the updated list
transforms.refutation: push changes the array in place and hands back only the new length, not the array.
transforms.rule: push returns the new length; the array changes in place.

transforms.belief: Appending a list adds its items one by one
transforms.refutation: push adds its argument as one item, so an array argument becomes a single nested item. Spread it with ... to add each.
transforms.rule: push(arr) adds one nested item; push(...arr) adds each.

transforms.belief: pop() removes the first item
transforms.refutation: pop works at the end of the array: it removes and returns the last item. shift is the one that takes the first.
transforms.rule: pop takes from the end; shift takes from the front.

templates.harness:
check(JSON.stringify({{@fn}}([{{a}}], [{{b}}, {{c}}])) === '[{{a}},{{b}},{{c}}]', 'adds each extra item');
check(JSON.stringify({{@fn}}([], [{{d}}])) === '[{{d}}]', 'starts from empty');

transforms.belief: b = a makes a separate copy of the list
transforms.refutation: const {{@b}} = {{@a}} copies only the reference: both names point to one array, so the push shows through {{@a}}.
transforms.rule: Assignment shares one array; [...a] makes a copy.

transforms.belief: A function gets its own copy of a list argument
transforms.refutation: The function receives the very array the caller has, not a copy, so the push inside {{@fn}} changes {{@xs}}.
transforms.rule: Arrays passed to functions are shared, not copied.

transforms.belief: Pointing a at a new list also changes b
transforms.refutation: The reassignment points {{@a}} at a brand-new array; {{@b}} still points at the old one, which nobody changed.
transforms.rule: Reassigning a name never changes what other names point to.

transforms.belief: Copying a list also copies the lists inside it
transforms.refutation: Spreading copies only the outer array; the inner rows are still shared, so the change shows in {{@grid}}.
transforms.rule: [...a] is shallow; inner arrays stay shared.

templates.rule: b = a shares one array; [...a] makes a new one.

transforms.belief: obj.key uses the value of the variable key
transforms.refutation: A dot always takes the name literally: {{@obj}}.{{@key}} reads the property called {{@key}}, ignoring the variable.
transforms.rule: obj.name is literal; obj[name] uses the variable value.

transforms.belief: obj[key] looks up a property literally named key
transforms.refutation: Brackets evaluate what is inside: [{{@key}}] uses the text stored in {{@key}}, while ['{{@key}}'] would be the literal name.
transforms.rule: obj[key] looks up the value stored in key.

transforms.belief: Reading a property of undefined just gives undefined
transforms.refutation: {{@user}} has no {{@prop}}, so the second dot asks a missing value for a property, which throws. ?. would stop safely.
transforms.rule: Reading a property of undefined throws; guard with ?.

transforms.belief: obj[1] and obj['1'] are different properties
transforms.refutation: Object keys are always text, so the number {{k}} becomes the key '{{k}}': both lines write the same property.
transforms.rule: Object keys are strings: obj[1] and obj['1'] are the same.

subgoals.label: A property name in a variable

transforms.belief: Defining a function runs its body
transforms.refutation: Defining {{@fn}} only stores it; its body runs each time {{@fn}}() is called, which happens only on the last line.
transforms.rule: A function body runs only when the function is called.

transforms.belief: Writing the name without () calls it
transforms.refutation: Without parentheses, {{@fn}} is the function itself, stored under a new name; only {{@fn}}() runs it.
transforms.rule: Add () to call a function; the bare name is the function.

transforms.belief: Arguments match parameters by the caller's variable names
transforms.refutation: Arguments fill parameters by position: the first value goes to {{@p1}}, whatever the caller's variable is called.
transforms.rule: Arguments match parameters by order, never by name.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}({{a}}, {{b}}) === {{e1}}, 'adds two squares');
check({{@fn}}({{c}}, {{d}}) === {{e2}}, 'adds two other squares');

transforms.belief: A function that prints gives back that value
transforms.refutation: console.log only shows the value on screen; a function gives nothing back unless it says return.
transforms.rule: Only return gives a value back to the caller.

transforms.belief: return shows the value on the screen
transforms.refutation: return hands the value back silently; the first call's result is thrown away because nothing logs it.
transforms.rule: return gives a value back; only console.log shows it.

transforms.belief: Lines after return still run
transforms.refutation: return ends the function at once, so the console.log after it can never run.
transforms.rule: Nothing after return runs in that call.

transforms.belief: return inside a loop only ends that pass
transforms.refutation: return leaves the whole function immediately, loop and all, the first time an item passes the test.
transforms.rule: return inside a loop ends the whole function.

templates.harness:
check({{@fn}}([{{a}}, {{b}}]) === {{s}}, 'gives back the sum');
check({{@fn}}([{{c}}]) === {{c}}, 'gives back a single value');

transforms.belief: map changes the original array
transforms.refutation: map builds a brand-new array from the results; {{@xs}} itself is left exactly as it was.
transforms.rule: map returns a new array; the original is unchanged.

transforms.belief: An arrow function with braces returns its last expression
transforms.refutation: With braces, an arrow function runs a block of statements and gives back nothing unless it says return.
transforms.rule: With braces, write return; without braces, the value returns.

transforms.belief: filter keeps the items where the test is false
transforms.refutation: filter keeps the items whose test comes out true and drops the rest.
transforms.rule: filter keeps the items that pass the test.

transforms.belief: reduce without a start value starts from 0
transforms.refutation: Without a start value, reduce starts from the first item itself and combines from the second item on.
transforms.rule: Without a start value, reduce begins with the first item.

templates.harness:
check(JSON.stringify({{@fn}}([{{a}}, -{{b}}, {{c}}], {{k}})) === '[{{ak}},{{ck}}]', 'scales the positive values');
check(JSON.stringify({{@fn}}([-{{a}}], {{k}})) === '[]', 'drops negatives');

transforms.belief: A method keeps its object as this when stored in a variable
transforms.refutation: this is decided by how a function is called: {{@fn}}() has no object before the dot, so this is not {{@obj}}.
transforms.rule: this is the object before the dot at call time.

transforms.belief: A regular function callback sees the outer method's this
transforms.refutation: A regular function passed as a callback gets its own this, not the method's; an arrow function would keep the outer this.
transforms.rule: Use an arrow callback to keep the method's this.

transforms.belief: this inside a method means the function itself
transforms.refutation: Called as {{@counter}}.bump(), the method gets {{@counter}} itself as this, the object before the dot, not the function.
transforms.rule: this is the object before the dot at call time.

templates.harness:
check(JSON.stringify({{@make}}({{k}}).scale([{{a}}, {{b}}])) === '[{{ak}},{{bk}}]', 'scales each value');
check(JSON.stringify({{@make}}({{m}}).scale([{{c}}])) === '[{{cm}}]', 'uses the factor of its own object');

transforms.belief: Each function made in a loop remembers that pass's value
transforms.refutation: var makes one i shared by every pass; each arrow reads i when it is called, after the loop has finished counting.
transforms.rule: Closures read a variable when they run, not when made.

transforms.belief: let and var behave the same in loop callbacks
transforms.refutation: A let loop variable is created fresh for each pass, so each arrow keeps its own i; var would share one.
transforms.rule: let gives each pass its own i; var shares one.

transforms.belief: Each function made in a loop remembers that pass's value
transforms.refutation: The callbacks run after the loop ends, and they all share the one var i, which by then has gone past {{n}}.
transforms.rule: Closures read a variable when they run, not when made.

templates.rule: var shares one i across passes; let makes one per pass.

transforms.belief: Annotating a value as number converts it to a number
transforms.refutation: : number only tells the type checker what to expect; the running program keeps the text exactly as it was.
transforms.rule: Annotations never change values; convert with Number() yourself.

transforms.replace: const {{@qty}}: number = {{@raw}}; if (typeof {{@qty}} !== 'number') throw new TypeError('{{@qty}} is not a number');
transforms.belief: Type annotations are checked while the program runs
transforms.refutation: Type annotations are erased before the code runs, so nothing checks {{@qty}} while the program runs.
transforms.rule: Types are checked by tsc before running, never during.

transforms.belief: x as number turns the value into a number
transforms.refutation: as number only silences the type checker; it is erased before running and never converts the text.
transforms.rule: as changes what tsc believes, never the value.

transforms.replace: JSON.parse('{"id": "{{a}}", "qty": {{q}}}'); if (typeof {{@item}}.id !== 'number') throw new TypeError('id is not a number');
transforms.belief: Type annotations are checked while the program runs
transforms.refutation: The interface is erased before running; JSON.parse returns whatever the text holds, and nothing checks it against {{@Item}}.
transforms.rule: Types are checked by tsc before running, never during.

transforms.belief: Annotating a value as number converts it to a number
transforms.refutation: Declaring id: number in {{@Item}} converts nothing; the parsed text value stays text.
transforms.rule: Annotations never change values; convert with Number() yourself.
